NOTES.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

We will study module 7a today about organic light emitting diodes.

Key details

  • This is the only class in this topic, and we are going to study about the construction, working, the types of OLEDs, the advantages, disadvantages, and applications.
  • The most common material is gallium arsenide, which is used to make these LEDs.
  • Further doping is done and we have different types of colored LEDs.
  • And they recombine in the depletion layer.
  • When they recombine, they give out a photon and that is what we see as light.
  • They use organic molecules and hence the name organic light emitting diodes.
  • The phenomena which is happening in OLEDs is called electroluminescence.
  • Therefore, OLEDs have an emissive electroluminescent layer, which is a film of an organic compound that emits light in response to an electric current.
  • Hence they are also known as organic electroluminescent diodes.
  • The first OLED device was made by Eastman Kodak in the nineteen eighties.
  • So we know Kodak Labs, it was first made there and it's an emerging technology for displays.
  • All of us have seen.
  • OLED TVs, so much advertisement for OLED mobile displays.
  • Because these displays can be flexible, they can be very thin and of light weight.
  • Moreover, the power consumption is less as compared to the conventional LEDs and the L C Ds.
  • Apart from that, they offer a high contrast, brighter displays with wider viewing angle.
  • And here you can actually roll it.
  • First of all, there is a substrate which is made of glass and that is basically for support.
  • On the substrate, we can see the anode.
  • This is usually transparent and made of indium tin oxide it is ITO and then we have two organic layers here as you can see this orange layer over here is known as the conductive layer and it is going to transport holes from the anode and this is usually made of polyaniline and also there are other material organic molecules which are used to make this conductive layer.
  • And then we also have the next layer which is again an organic mole made of organic molecules and this is known as the emissive layer.
  • And here we have these this is very important because this is where the light emission happens.

Example or application from the lecture

  • First, let us understand the working of light emitting diodes, because the same concept can be extended to organic light emitting diodes.
  • Let us understand the construction.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

and light is emitted.

Key details

  • And the cathode of course is used to inject electrons and it is usually made with metals like magnesium which have a low work function.
  • A voltage is applied across the anode and cathode of the OLED.
  • We can see that the cathode will be connected to the negative terminal, hence there are.
  • Electrons coming from the cathode.
  • The green layer you can see here, these are moving to the emissive layers from emissive layer from the cathode.
  • And at the same time, electrons.
  • which have moved out of this orange layer over here which is the conductive layer.
  • So therefore what happens?
  • Holes have now moved into the conductive layer.
  • You can see here closer to the emissive layer and therefore light is being emitted from the emissive layer.
  • And the intensity of the light, that is the brightness of the light, is going to depend on the current density.
  • These two are going the holes in the electrons are going to combine and this combination happens closer to the emissive layer and that is how whenever there's a combination of a electron and a hole then there will be emission of light.
  • And the holes are at a lower energy level.
  • We have learned this in right from spectros molecular spectroscopy when we were studying.
  • We have passive matrix OLED, which is known as the emolet, and we have the active matrix OLED, that is the emolet.
  • Then we have transparent OLEDs, we have foldable O LED, we have top emitting OLED and white O LED.
  • The first one is a passive matrix O LED, and here we have strips of these cathode.
  • and anode and the organic layers.
  • The anode strips are arranged perpendicular to the cathode strips and the intersection of the cathode and anode they form the pixels from where the light is emitted.

Example or application from the lecture

  • One example of a polymer which is used.
  • Whenever there is an electron transition from a higher level to the lower level, the energy is given out in the form of a radiation, and here it is in the visible region.
  • Let us look at each one of them carefully what are these different types of O LEDs which we are referring to.

Core explanation · 10:00–14:59

There has to be an external circuitry here which applies current to selected strips of anode and cathode, thereby determining which pixel should be turned on and which pixel should be turned off.

Key details

  • So because of this external circuitry here, the power consumption is more compared to the other OLEDs, and therefore these are mostly used for small screens.
  • Coming to active matrix OLEDs which are more popular and many of the mobile displays now they use this amulet.
  • They have a full layer of cathode, organic molecules, and anode.
  • Here the anode layer has a thin film transistor TFT array at the back plate.
  • There is a back plate of TFT and that forms a matrix.
  • Now amulets therefore consume less power than the P amulets because the TFT array requires less power as compared to the external circuitry and therefore they are very efficient for large displays.
  • like we have electronic signages or we have these big TVs, large screen TVs.
  • They consist of a transparent substrate, cathode and anode.
  • And a transparent OLED display can be either active matrix type or a passive matrix type.
  • And it is used in transparent projector screens and glasses.
  • The next one is a top editing OLED.
  • They are best suited for active metrics design and they are used for making small card displays.
  • Then foldable O LEDs.
  • They have the substrate made of very flexible metal foils or plastics, as you can see here, and they are very lightweight, ultra thin and because they are foldable they can reduce the breakage of displays.
  • Personal digital assistance.
  • They give you true color quality like of incandescent lighting, and therefore they can be used for large and efficient lighting systems.
  • The organic lay of an OLED are thinner, lighter, and more flexible than the crystalline layers of LED or L CD.
  • We know that in the market we have L C D or.
  • TVs and then came the LED TVs.
  • And now there's a lot of talk about O LED screens.
  • They are brighter than LEDs because the organic layer of an O LED are much thinner than the corresponding inorganic crystal layers which are used in LED.
  • And so the conductive and the emissing emissive lay of an OLED can be multi-layered.
  • And of course they consume much less power than the L C D's.
  • and then easier to produce and can be made in large sizes and they have large fields of view.
  • In an L C D we know that if we go at an angle we will not be able to see the picture.
  • That is not the case with O L E D.
  • Up to 170 degrees the viewing angle has now become very large and there's a very high color contrast and faster response time.
  • They have shorter lifespan and the manufacturing process is expensive.
  • And one of the most important problem we face with OLEDs is water can easily damage them.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us see what are the advantages of OLEDs.

Core explanation · 15:00–19:59

What are the applications?

Key details

  • They are used in mobile phone displays.
  • And then we have digital cameras where they can be used.
  • As we said, white bullets, they can be used for lighting.
  • Then we have audio video players and then we have OLED TVs and then also different.
  • Other type of devices like wristwatches, so displays in wristwatches, etc.
  • And if they are foldable, you can put it right over your wrist.
  • And in the next class we will be talking about green chemistry, which is the last class of unit five.
